comparison: Both evaluate claims about reduced diversity, clonal expansion, and repertoire characteristics in foetal TCRβ (C13-C16, C62-C67). OpenEval also includes TCRα diversity claims (C68-C72) which peer reviewers address in the same result. Both find these claims SUPPORTED and note consistency with previous studies.

OpenEval evaluates TCRα repertoire differences (C68-C72) as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers include these claims in their broader evaluation of diversity findings (R1), acknowledging both TCRβ and TCRα repertoire characteristics as consistent with prior work.

Perfect alignment on claims C1-C2, C73-C76 regarding life-stage clustering and chromosomal location bias. Both find these claims SUPPORTED. Reviewers acknowledge this as a key finding with comprehensive analysis, though note concerns about generalizability beyond the E18.5 timepoint.

Both evaluate chromosomal location-dependent bias in gene segment usage (C3-C5, C77-C78). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by heatmap and gene usage data. Peer reviewers also acknowledge this finding as SUPPORTED, explicitly noting the 3'TRAV/5'TRAJ bias in foetal cells versus 5'TRAV preference in adults.

Major disagreement on interpretation. OpenEval finds claims about reduced progressive rearrangement (C6, C79-C82) SUPPORTED, noting the inference is reasonable given known biology. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, explicitly stating claims about progressive TCRα rearrangements are 'oversimplified and potentially misleading' due to single-timepoint analysis.

Perfect alignment on TRBJ cluster usage claims (C83-C85). Both find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the inference about positive selection is reasonable; peer reviewers do not specifically critique this finding and treat it as part of the comprehensive analysis.

Both address PCA findings showing life-stage differences (C86-C90). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED with clear clustering patterns. Peer reviewers include these claims in their broader evaluation of MHC-restriction findings (R6), acknowledging the data as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate CDR3 length differences (C96-C98). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED and notes consistency with previous reports. Peer reviewers also acknowledge these findings as SUPPORTED, noting they are 'in line with previous studies' and represent confirmatory results.

Both address repertoire sharing via Jaccard indices (C99-C101). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED, indicating greater sequence sharing in foetal samples. Peer reviewers include these in their evaluation of repertoire characteristics, treating them as valid confirmatory findings consistent with prior work.

Both evaluate cell-type segregation and MHC-restriction effects (C9-C12, C104-C109). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by PCA and heatmap data. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a key finding, stating 'positive selection of foetal thymocytes are less dependent on interactions with the MHC' and rating it SUPPORTED.

Both address differential MHC-restriction influence on TCRα (C111-C114). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by PCA showing adult SP separation versus dispersed foetal populations. Peer reviewers include this in their broader MHC-restriction evaluation, acknowledging 'Effects of MHC-restriction were notably weaker in fetal thymocytes.'

Both evaluate quantitative differences in MHC-restriction variance (C115-C118). OpenEval finds the 4-fold calculation SUPPORTED despite different PCs being compared. Peer reviewers include this in their comprehensive acknowledgment of weaker MHC-restriction effects in foetal thymocytes, rating it SUPPORTED.

Both address failure of foetal populations to segregate by cell-type in TCRα VxJ analysis (C119-C120). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as strong evidence for differential MHC-restriction. Peer reviewers include this in their broader MHC-restriction findings, acknowledging it as SUPPORTED.

Both evaluate quantitative differences in MHC-restriction for TCRα CDR1xCDR2 (C121-C123). OpenEval finds the 2-fold difference SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers include this in their comprehensive evaluation of MHC-restriction effects, acknowledging these findings as SUPPORTED.

Both address lack of foetal cell-type separation in TCRα V region analysis (C124-C126). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as converging evidence for weaker MHC-restriction. Peer reviewers include this in their broader acknowledgment of MHC-restriction findings, rating it SUPPORTED.

Perfect alignment on hydrocortisone experiment claims (C7-C8, C134-C137). Both find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this provides strong evidence for differentiation kinetics influence. Peer reviewers acknowledge the repertoire became 'more foetal like' after HC treatment, supporting the kinetics hypothesis.

Both address inferences about differentiation kinetics (C149-C150). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by HC experiment and known biology. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, questioning whether conclusions about progressive rearrangements are justified given single-timepoint analysis, despite acknowledging the HC data.

Both evaluate overarching conclusions (C138, C143). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by comprehensive characterization. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, expressing concern about overgeneralization and stating conclusions are 'oversimplified and potentially misleading' given single-timepoint analysis.

Both address speculation about progressive rearrangements (C130). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN, noting the claim is speculative despite indirect HC support. Peer reviewers also rate related claims UNCERTAIN, explicitly challenging the interpretation as 'oversimplified and potentially misleading' due to methodological limitations.

Both address speculation about evolutionary significance (C142). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN, noting lack of direct functional evidence. Peer reviewers also express concern about overgeneralization of functional conclusions, questioning whether broad statements about foetal T-cell properties are justified.

Both address speculation about clonal expansion mechanisms (C144). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN, noting lack of direct measurement of proliferation. Peer reviewers also question broad functional conclusions, expressing concern about overgeneralization from the single-timepoint data.

OpenEval evaluates specific VxJ combinations with life-stage differences (C91-C95) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these claims, though they relate to the broader gene segment usage findings acknowledged by reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about TCR diversity and V(D)J recombination (C17-C25) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these established background claims.
OpenEval evaluates background claims about developmental biology and thymus timing (C26-C34) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these contextual claims.
OpenEval evaluates established immunology background (C35-C44) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these mechanistic context claims.
OpenEval evaluates established differences between foetal and adult thymus (C45-C55) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these background claims.
OpenEval evaluates prior knowledge about TCR repertoires (C56-C61) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these foundational claims.
OpenEval evaluates structural immunology background (C102-C103, C110) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these contextual claims.
OpenEval evaluates established molecular biology of TCR rearrangement (C127-C129) as SUPPORTED by appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these mechanistic background claims.
OpenEval evaluates claims about human development parallels (C147-C148) as SUPPORTED by citation to Park et al., 2020. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these comparative claims.

OpenEval evaluates future research directions regarding single-cell approaches (C152) as SUPPORTED as a reasonable limitation acknowledgment. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate this methodological limitation statement.
